title: Check it against the texts
hook: the four great references: test any claimed teaching against the discourses and the discipline
carry: set the words beside the discourses

segments.voice: Yesterday: acariyamutthi, and the Buddha's open hand at Beluva. Your line: an open hand in both directions. Today: if nothing is secret, how do you spot a fake?

A screenshot is going around. A famous quote, a soft background, a name underneath: the Buddha. Did he actually say it? Most people have no idea how to check, and the quote travels anyway. This is not a new problem. The Buddha knew that after he was gone people would say, I heard this from his own lips. So on the road north, at a town called Bhoganagara, he gave the monks a method. Four situations, one test.
screen: `A QUOTE WITH HIS NAME ON IT.` → `I HEARD IT FROM HIM.` → `A METHOD AT BHOGANAGARA.`

segments.voice: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta calls them the four great references, the mahapadesa. Suppose a monk says: I heard this from the Blessed One himself; this is the teaching, this is the discipline. Or: I heard it from a whole community, with its elders. Or: from a group of learned elders who know the texts by heart. Or: from one learned elder. Four sources, from the most impressive to the most modest. And the instruction is the same for all four. Don't welcome it, and don't scorn it. Learn the words carefully, then set them beside the discourses and compare them with the discipline. If they don't fit, conclude: this isn't the Buddha's word; this monk got it wrong. Set it aside. If they do fit, conclude: this is the Buddha's word; he got it right. Look at what the test doesn't care about. Not how famous the speaker is. Not how many people agree. Not even the claim, I heard it from him. The words themselves are checked against the body of teaching everyone can hear. It's yesterday's open hand, turned into a safeguard. Because nothing was secret, everything can be compared. Over the centuries, different Buddhist traditions have worked out which texts count as the measure, and they don't all draw that line in the same place. But the habit itself, check it against what's been taught, goes back to this road.
screen: `FOUR CLAIMS, ONE TEST.` · `DON'T APPLAUD, DON'T SCORN.` · `SET IT BESIDE THE DISCOURSES.` · `THE WORDS, NOT THE SPEAKER.` · then, large: `CHECK IT AGAINST THE TEXTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one saying you've heard attributed to the Buddha, or to any teacher you respect, and hold it lightly, neither approving nor rejecting it. Just notice whether you know where it comes from. Then let the question rest, and stay with the breath.
Mahapadesa. The four great references in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta: whoever claims a teaching, set the words beside the discourses and the discipline. Today's word.
Your line: set the words beside the discourses. The words get checked, not the speaker. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist scholars and teachers still appeal to the four great references when weighing a disputed teaching, and different traditions define the body of texts used as the measure in their own ways.

fork.setup: a respected elder tells you a teaching he says the Buddha gave. you've never heard it. what do the four great references say to do?
options: reject it: you haven't heard it.
learn the words, then compare them with the discourses and the discipline.

original.note: Pali mahapadesa: a great reference, a standard to appeal to. DN 16 gives four.

trapdoor: what you thought: if someone important says the Buddha said it, he said it.
what it means: every claim, whoever makes it, is checked against the discourses and the discipline.

what a scholar hears: the mahapadesa passage (sutte otaretabbani, vinaye sandassetabbani) is one of the earliest hermeneutic rules in the canon, and later traditions applied it to their own scriptural collections.

chat.meaning: The four great references: whoever claims a teaching, neither applaud nor scorn. Learn the words and check them against the discourses and the discipline.
